keyVerseText: Thou shalt be hid from the scourge of the tongue: neither shalt thou be afraid of destruction when it cometh. from: or, when the tongue scourgeth
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun שֹׁד (shôd) derives from the root שׁוּד (shûwd), which literally means to waste or swell up, figuratively extending to devastate or ruin. This root sense conveys not merely physical destruction but an active, overwhelming devastation that can imply insolence or violent spoiling. The literal idea of swelling or expanding destruction adds a vivid image of ruin spreading uncontrollably, deepening the common English glosses of desolation and spoil.
usageInScripture: Throughout its 25 occurrences, שֹׁד consistently conveys themes of violence, devastation, oppression, and spoil. The top translations such as 'and spoil,' 'wasting,' and 'destruction' highlight its use in contexts of social sin and ruin, whether referring to nations, individuals, or even beasts. This range shows the word's flexibility in describing both physical devastation and moral or social havoc, underscoring a comprehensive understanding of ruin in biblical narrative.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding שֹׁד as encompassing both violent destruction and social sin enriches our grasp of biblical judgment and human brokenness. It reveals how sin not only harms individuals but also devastates communities and nations, reflecting the pervasive consequences of rebellion against God. The word's depth reminds believers that God's justice addresses both external ruin and internal corruption, pointing ultimately to Christ's redeeming work that overcomes devastation and restores what was spoiled. This term calls the faithful to trust in God's protection from such ruin and to live in the hope of His restorative power.
keyVerseReflection: Job 5:21 promises protection from the 'scourge of the tongue' and assures that the believer will not fear 'destruction when it cometh.' Here, שֹׁד conveys the looming threat of ruin or devastation that can arise from harmful words or circumstances. The verse uses this word to emphasize God's safeguarding power over both social and personal havoc, encouraging trust that God hides His people from the destructive forces symbolized by שֹׁד.
